modules.module: M1: What Makes Something an Agent

Claude.notes: Foundational definitions (Russell-Norvig, PEAS, autonomy spectrum, specification problem, environment taxonomy) are structurally sound and appropriately Advanced. Case studies (ChatGPT function-calling, Zillow iBuying $304M, CoastRunners, Flash Crash) hook each concept, but the concepts are usually declared before the story fully creates the felt-tension — narrative works as illustration more than induction.
Claude.topIssue: Definitions are stated before the story lets the learner feel why they matter — L1 gives Russell-Norvig up front rather than letting the ChatGPT plugin threshold produce the definition.

Gemini.notes: Technical framing is largely correct but carries small factual slippages. Russell & Norvig's AIMA first edition is 1995 (not 1994 as suggested); the paper 'AI Safety and the Problem of Corrigibility' is not a canonical Anthropic publication — corrigibility framing traces to Soares/Fallenstein 2015 and Anthropic's Constitutional AI (2022). Instrumental convergence is well-explained but the standard attribution is Omohundro (2008) and Bostrom (2012), not primarily Armstrong.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Anthropic 2022 corrigibility paper' referenced in L2 does not correspond to a real Anthropic publication with that title; corrigibility posture is discussed in Anthropic's HH-RLHF and Constitutional AI work, but the citation-shaped claim overstates the paper trail.

Perplexity.notes: The canonical cases (Flash Crash 2010, CoastRunners 2016, Zillow Q3 2021, Waymo SF Level 4, Air Canada BC tribunal 2024) are appropriate anchor points. But by mid-2026 a learner would expect explicit mention of Anthropic's Computer Use, MCP, and Claude Opus 4 as the current agent-threshold examples rather than 'ChatGPT + function-calling June 2023' as the leading-edge illustration.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 'crossed the agent threshold' story stops at June 2023 function-calling — no reference to Anthropic Computer Use (Oct 2024) or MCP (late 2024), both of which are now the reference points for what a modern agent's actuator surface looks like.

Claude.notes: The WebArena 14% opening does exactly what the module needs — the number sets up 'why is browser navigation hard?' before the perception/planning/action loop is unpacked. Lab scenarios (flight booking, benefits form with CAPTCHA + 20-min timeout, corporate email/calendar agent) are highly specific and give the AI tutor real ground to push back on.
Claude.topIssue: The insight arc from grounding failure → recovery is stated more than earned — learners are told 'grounding failures are the most common cause of browser agent errors' rather than experiencing it inside a lab replay.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of accessibility tree, action space, grounding, and prompt-injection surfaces are accurate. The WebArena baseline (14%), Playwright/Selenium/Puppeteer stack, and OpenAI Operator / Anthropic Computer Use framing are correct. The three ways of seeing a webpage (HTML/DOM, screenshot, accessibility tree) matches how research agents like SeeAct, WebVoyager, and Anthropic's Computer Use actually operate.
Gemini.topIssue: Prompt-injection defenses named in L4 do not distinguish 'system-prompt hardening' (limited defense) from 'trust-boundary redesign' (the actual mitigation) — a technically loose framing that could mislead a builder into over-trusting instruction hierarchies.

Perplexity.notes: Browser-agent coverage is current: Operator, Computer Use, Playwright/Selenium/Puppeteer are still the tools of the trade in 2026. Lab scenarios (govt benefits form, corporate support agent) map cleanly to what teams actually deploy this year.
Perplexity.topIssue: Anthropic Computer Use is named but not treated as the reference platform it has become by 2026; the module still centers OpenAI Operator as the flagship browser-agent case where a 2026 reader would expect them side-by-side.

Claude.notes: The strongest lab set in the course. Each scenario is a specific artifact a real product lead would recognize — the mid-size outdoor-gear e-commerce brief, the 14-unauthorized-refunds incident report, the '62% deflection but 8% churn' metrics tension, and the handoff design brief. Klarna Feb 2024 (two-thirds of chats, 11min → 2min) opens the module with a number that carries the whole architecture argument.
Claude.topIssue: The three-generation history (rule-based → intent-classification → agentic) is clean but understated on the sunk-cost problem — real deployments still run all three simultaneously, and the module could do more to prepare learners for the archaeology of a working stack.

Gemini.notes: Klarna case is materially accurate — the Feb 2024 announcement did claim two-thirds handling and ~2min avg vs 11min prior. Dialogflow/LUIS references are correct for Gen-2. Terminology (tool use, escalation logic, deflection rate) is used correctly at the practitioner level.
Gemini.topIssue: The '14 refunds' incident lab implies policy enforcement is a prompt-engineering problem, but in production this is enforced at the tool-schema / capability-scoping layer — the technical framing understates the architectural fix.

Perplexity.notes: The Klarna reference is still the canonical Gen-3 customer-service case study in 2026 — a good anchor. The 62% deflection / 8% churn tension is exactly the KPI conflict practitioners are debating right now. Labs generalize cleanly to Zendesk, Intercom Fin, and Sierra deployments live in the market.
Perplexity.topIssue: Klarna's 2024 walk-back on agent deployment (reversing some of the automation after quality complaints, reported later in 2024/2025) is not mentioned — a learner reading in 2026 would benefit from the second half of that story.

Claude.notes: Devin/SWE-bench opens with a specific number (13.86%) rather than a vague capability claim — that discipline shows throughout. Distinction between suggestion tools (Copilot) and execution agents (Devin, SWE-agent, Replit Agent) is well-drawn, and the tool-design lab is one of the more concretely productive exercises in the course.
Claude.topIssue: The 'observe → plan → act' loop is stated as canonical but the module doesn't show a learner what a broken loop looks like — a walk-through of a real coding-agent trace where the plan step drifts would sharpen the payoff.

Gemini.notes: Devin's SWE-bench 13.86% is technically correct; the Cognition demo cherry-picking was documented by Ziegler and others in April 2024. Tool inventory (bash, editor, browser, linter, git) matches how SWE-agent and Aider are actually built.
Gemini.topIssue: Copilot's June 2021 launch and the framing of it as purely 'next-token' predict does not reflect Copilot Workspace / Copilot Agent evolution — the boundary between 'autocomplete' and 'agent' is now more porous than the module suggests.

Perplexity.notes: Coding-agent landscape is well-covered for mid-2024, and most of the tools named (Devin, SWE-agent, Aider, Replit Agent) are still current in 2026. SWE-bench remains the reference benchmark, and the leaderboard-inflation critique still applies.
Perplexity.topIssue: Claude Code and Cursor Composer / Cursor Agent are absent from the coding-agent census — both are now larger-share systems than Devin, and their absence dates the module.

Claude.notes: Four-stage loop (decompose → retrieve → evaluate → synthesize) is a serviceable spine. Sydney/Bing opener is evocative but the story-to-concept handoff is thinner than in M2–M4 — the module leans on enumeration of vendors more than on a felt failure that the loop then explains.
Claude.topIssue: The Sydney/Bing opener creates a strong image but never resolves into a design lesson — the story does not translate into 'that's why research agents need a re-query gate.'

Gemini.notes: Perplexity 'query fan-out' 3–7 sub-queries and OpenAI Deep Research 'browse dozens of URLs per task' are directionally correct but presented as harder claims than the public documentation supports. FRAMES benchmark is real but the pass-rate framing is imprecise.
Gemini.topIssue: Claims like Perplexity generating 3–7 sub-queries per user question are presented as fact but come from external observation and vary considerably by mode; the module treats vendor-observed heuristics as documented architecture.

Perplexity.notes: OpenAI Deep Research (Feb 2025) is included but the module still opens with Sydney/Bing (Feb 2023), which reads as a museum piece in 2026. Anthropic's Research capability and Perplexity Pro's Sonar are the current reference points a learner would expect to see contrasted.
Perplexity.topIssue: The Sydney/Bing 2023 opener anchors the module in a two-year-old moment; a 2026 reader would open with Deep Research + Anthropic Research + Perplexity Sonar as the current live three-way comparison.

Claude.notes: The AutoGPT 150k-stars-in-two-months opener carries real weight, and the three-constraint framing (context exhaustion, skill mismatch, no parallelism) gives the module a clean argument. Orchestration patterns (hub-and-spoke, pipeline, blackboard) are a good taxonomy.
Claude.topIssue: The 'GPT-4 8k context' framing dates the constraint story — the underlying insight (context boundaries force decomposition) survives, but the exact numbers pull the module toward 2023.

Gemini.notes: AutoGen, LangGraph, and Rufus hub-and-spoke framing are accurate. Devin's structured-message-bus vs shared-context claim is directionally right but simplifies a design that Cognition has publicly discussed only in outline.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Devin agents communicated through a structured message bus rather than shared context' claim is presented as documented architecture but Cognition has never published that internal design detail — it is inference from behavior.

Perplexity.notes: Multi-agent design patterns (hub-and-spoke, pipeline, blackboard) still hold in 2026, but the specific stack callouts skip Anthropic's Sub-agents / Claude Code teams, LangGraph 1.0, and CrewAI's 2025 v0.100 series that dominate current implementations.
Perplexity.topIssue: AutoGPT-era anchors (May 2023 postmortems, 8k context) tell an accurate but two-generation-old story — the current framing would be Claude Code sub-agents, LangGraph, and CrewAI at production scale.

Claude.notes: The strongest narrative-to-concept coupling in the course. OpenAI hide-and-seek → ramp surfing → Krakovna's specification-gaming list is a case that creates the exact problem the concept section resolves. The corrigibility lab (24/7 autonomous cloud infra) is one of the sharpest scenarios in the deck.
Claude.topIssue: Some overlap with M1's specification/reward-hacking coverage — the two modules could be more explicitly cross-referenced so learners see M7 as the operational deepening rather than a re-introduction.

Gemini.notes: Krakovna's spec-gaming list, CoastRunners, Tetris pause-to-avoid-loss, and moveable-ramp exploit are all accurately described and correctly attributed. The prompt-injection framing (indirect injection via retrieved content) matches Greshake et al. 2023.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'objective misspecification' vs 'reward hacking' vs 'specification gaming' distinction is technically correct but the module uses the terms as near-synonyms in places where the sub-distinctions matter for evaluation design.

Perplexity.notes: Specification gaming is a durable failure class — the canonical examples (CoastRunners, hide-and-seek, Tetris) age well, and the corrigibility framing is still the practical reference. Indirect prompt injection remains a live 2026 threat.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 2025–2026 wave of documented agent-injection incidents (retrieval-poisoned tool calls, memory-poisoning attacks in long-running agents) is not mentioned; the injection story stops at the classical email/browser cases.

Claude.notes: The 'Devin March 2024 → Ziegler April 2024 replication' arc lets the module do exactly what it should — introduce a frontier claim, then invite skepticism, then resolve into a technique (long-horizon planning, memory stores, verification loops). Labs mirror this: build for long horizons, then defend against emergent coordination.
Claude.topIssue: The 'road ahead' section (L4) leans harder on Anthropic and OpenAI product roadmaps than on the underlying technical trajectories — a learner would benefit from a sharper distinction between company plans and capability trajectories.

Gemini.notes: Devin SWE-bench 13.86% is technically correct and the Ziegler cherry-picking replication is real. Long-horizon planning ingredients (persistent memory, structured planning, verified tool use, larger contexts) match the practitioner literature. Emergent-coordination discussion in L2 is accurate but tucked behind broad framing.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'scalable oversight' framing invokes Bowman et al. 2022 without naming it, and the exact recursive-reward-modeling / debate distinction is elided — a technical audience would want that lineage spelled out.

Perplexity.notes: Most future-looking of the eight modules and holds up in 2026: long-horizon planning, computer use, multi-agent coordination, and oversight are still the frontier categories today. The Devin post-hype framing has aged into the mainstream view.
Perplexity.topIssue: The computer-use section still speaks of Anthropic Computer Use in an early-preview register; by mid-2026 it and OpenAI Operator are production surfaces with documented incident histories that would refresh the module.
